name: Cream blush

card.summary: A creamy cheek colour that blends into the skin for a natural flush, used to add warmth and a healthy, youthful look to the face.
card.note: Wears off with washing; patch-test if prone to reactions.

quick.overview:
Cream blush is a blush in a cream, stick, pot or liquid form that is dabbed onto the cheeks. Because it is moist, it sits in the skin and reads as a natural flush rather than a powder layer, which is why people use it to look healthier, warmer or more awake.

Blush in general has a long history, from ancient Egyptian red ochre mixed with fat to modern shades from pink to brown and orange. Cream versions are one of several modern formats alongside powder, liquid and gel.
quick.how: Users apply it with fingers, a sponge or a brush on the apples of the cheeks or higher on the cheekbones, often before powder and blended outward. Placement is said to change the face: higher and more sweeping to emphasize cheekbones, rounder on the apples for a youthful look. Effects last the day and are removed with normal cleansing.
quick.risks: Risks are those of cosmetics generally: skin irritation or allergy to an ingredient, breakouts for people sensitive to heavier formulas, and uneven colour if over-applied. Historic rouges used toxic ingredients such as red lead and cinnabar, which modern products do not.

lead: Cream blush is a cheek colour in a creamy or balmy texture, sold as sticks, pots or tubes. It is used to give the face a flush of colour that appears to come from the skin itself, adding warmth and what many describe as a healthy or youthful look.[1]

Blush as a category is ancient. Wikipedia reports that people in ancient Egypt mixed fat with red ochre for cheek and lip colour, and that rouge in China dates to the Shang dynasty and used safflower. Modern blush comes as powder, cream, liquid or gel and ranges across pink, red, brown and orange shades.[1] Cream formats are used for the natural finish, and are often applied with fingers or a sponge.
No studies were found on cream blush specifically. Its appearance purpose is cosmetic: colour and contour on the cheeks, which cosmetic references say is meant to accentuate facial bone structure.[1]

angle.text: It adds colour to the cheeks immediately and can be placed to suggest cheekbone shape. The effect lasts until it is washed off.

paras: Blush is also known as rouge or blusher and is used on the cheeks and sometimes the lips. It exists as powder, cream, liquid and gel; modern powder blushes are mostly talc-based, while cream versions are lipstick-like or balm-like products.[1]

Cheek colouring has been used in many cultures. Ancient Egyptians used fat with red ochre, Greeks used crushed mulberries and beet juice, and Chinese rouge was made from safflower. Roman mixtures used red lead and cinnabar and were later linked to serious health harms. In sixteenth-century Europe women applied heavy rouge over pale powdered faces.[1]

Users apply cream blush to add warmth and freshness, to create the impression of higher cheekbones, or to make skin look less tired. It is applied by hand or tool and can be blended into foundation for a skin-like finish. Wikipedia describes blush as intended to accentuate bone structure.[1]

timeline.event: Red ochre and fat used as cheek colour in ancient Egypt.[1]
Rouge made from safflower in China.[1]
